taxonomy.note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Solidago nemoralis and lists Texas in its native range. Modern treatments may split western former infraspecific concepts such as decemflora; preserve current accepted-name distinctions rather than blindly inheriting old broad concepts.

target_zone_range.evidence_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Natural Purola Plants list includes Solidago nemoralis as a natural Hays County plant. Travis — UT PRC Travis County herbarium specimen index includes Solidago nemoralis. Williamson — UT PRC Vascular Plants of Williamson County includes a field-based treatment of Solidago nemoralis. USDA-derived county data also supports numerous additional target-zone counties.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Do not transfer records assigned to currently accepted Solidago decemflora or Solidago mollis into S. nemoralis without checking the taxon concept.

morphology.look_here_first: Start low on the plant. Gray/old-field goldenrod is comparatively short and gray-hairy, with a densely pubescent stem and narrow spatulate-to-oblanceolate lower leaves that become smaller and narrower upward. Then check the usually one-sided, wandlike/recurving flowering branches and the phyllaries.
best_field_traits: usually shorter and less colony-forming than tall goldenrods
lower leaves oblanceolate to spatulate, narrowed into a winged petiole
upper leaves progressively smaller and narrow
flowering array often one-sided and wandlike/recurving
dry open prairie, caliche, glade, old-field or roadside setting
morphology.key_separation: Against S. radula, S. nemoralis is more gray/strigose overall and typically has a more wandlike, one-sided inflorescence; S. radula is conspicuously scabrous/hispid with broader lower leaves and a more compact terminal panicle. Against tall goldenrods, S. nemoralis is shorter with persistent gray pubescence and narrower lower foliage.
